Kremenets Jewish Cemetery

Jewish Cemetery · Ternopilska oblast, Ukraine

Demolished. This record shows a tension worth noting: it is categorized as 'fenced and protected,' yet the source's demolished field marks it as 'yes.' Kremenets, first documented in 1438, had representatives who participated in the Council of Four Lands, the major Jewish self-governing body of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. A Hasidic community was headed here in the late 18th century by Mordehai (1746–1820), son of Ihla-Mihla of Zolochiv, documented elsewhere in this collection, and I.B. Levinson contributed significantly to the Haskalah movement. By 1910, local Jews owned nearly all the town's trade and industry, including five hotels, four printing houses, and a match factory; two Yiddish periodicals, Kremenitser Shtime and Kremenitser Vohenblat, were published in the 1930s. In May 1919, Jews were massacred by the army of the Directorate of Ukraine. In August 1941, during active occupation rather than afterward, a synagogue and this very cemetery were demolished; the ghetto's liquidation in August 1942 saw more than 6,400 people murdered.
